Merge pull request #6 from GoogleCloudPlatform/okf-iso-datetimes

Make every timestamp an ISO 8601 datetime with an explicit offset

drop the timestamp conformance bullet from SPEC 11

Section 5 already states the format every timestamp-valued key uses. The
consumer MUST in section 11 and the matching justification in 5.5 restated
it twice more, so both go, along with the code comments that cited the
bullet by number.

is_stale is unchanged: it still ignores a value that carries no explicit
offset, since a date-only 2026-12-31 names a different instant in every
timezone.

drop the duplicated timestamp conformance prose from SPEC 5

The consumer rule and its rationale were stated twice: once in the 5
preamble and once as a conformance bullet in 11. 11 is where the other
consumer MUSTs live, so the preamble now states the format only.

make every timestamp an ISO 8601 datetime with an explicit offset

OKF v0.2 mixed two time formats. `generated.at` and `verified[].at` were
datetimes, while `stale_after`, `sources[].last_modified`, and
`usage_window.from`/`to` were bare dates. For `stale_after` that is
ambiguous, not just untidy: `2026-12-31` names a different instant in
every timezone, so the same bundle can be stale in one office and fresh
in another. The v0.3 proposal already files this as an open issue.

The SPEC now states the convention once in the §5 preamble: every
timestamp-valued key is an ISO 8601 datetime with an explicit UTC offset,
and §11 requires consumers to ignore anything else, a date-only value
included. Strict rather than lenient, because a midnight-UTC fallback
would silently reintroduce the disagreement it is meant to remove. The
§9 log date headings are unchanged; they group a day's entries and are
not field values.

The acme_retail bundle moves to the `T00:00:00Z` form, as do the SPEC
examples.

On the Python side this exposed a live bug. PyYAML follows YAML 1.1, so
`safe_load` coerced both forms into date/datetime objects and `safe_dump`
wrote them back as `2026-06-30 14:00:00+00:00`: the reference agent was
already corrupting `generated.at` on any bundle it rewrote, which is
visible in the committed viz.html files. Making `stale_after` a datetime
would also have walked `is_stale` into a `date >= datetime` TypeError.
Dropping the timestamp resolver from the loader keeps every frontmatter
value the string the author wrote, matching the YAML 1.2 core schema the
TypeScript side already uses, and makes the round-trip value-preserving.
`is_stale` then takes a `now: datetime` and rejects any value without a
`T` separator or an offset.

The regenerated stackoverflow viz.html also picks up a tags fix that
predates this change; the committed copy was stale.

Verified end to end against Dataplex: push and pull of acme_retail is
17 files, 17 ok, 0 lossy, and the stored aspect holds `stale_after`,
`last_modified`, and `usage_window` verbatim.

Restore the full repository contents

Adds back everything held on full-content while the repository was under
approval review: SPEC.md, the four example bundles, the sample configurations,
the reference_agent source and tests, and the Knowledge Catalog connector doc.

Restores the tree the repository had at dd6d846, so the relative links in the
README resolve again. Pure addition -- README.md, LICENSE.md and
CONTRIBUTING.md are unchanged.

Initial commit

README, license and contributing guide only, for repository approval review.

The specification, four example bundles, sample configurations, reference_agent
source and tests, and the Knowledge Catalog connector doc are held on the
full-content branch and land here once the repository is approved. README links
to those paths and they will not resolve until then.

is the canonical home of the spec, the reference agent, and the sample

okf: rename enrichment_agent package to reference_agent (#129)

Reframes the OKF proof-of-concept agent as the reference agent to
disambiguate it from other agents and to match how it is described in
the README. All Python imports, ADK identifiers, CLI script, PyPI dist
name, User-Agent string, prompt filename, and prose in READMEs are
updated. SPEC.md is unchanged.

Fix OKF cross-links to use file-relative paths so bundles render on GitHub (#45)

* Emit OKF cross-links as file-relative paths

Previously the enrichment agent emitted every concept cross-link as a
bundle-root-absolute path (`/tables/users.md`). That form breaks when
the bundle is browsed on GitHub, where a leading `/` is interpreted as
repo-root-relative and every link 404s. Fix by switching the emitter,
prompt guidance, and viewer over to file-relative paths, and
regenerating the checked-in bundles.

Code:
- bundle/index.py: write paths relative to the index file's own
  directory (`foo.md`, `subdir/index.md`) instead of `/path`.
- viewer/generator.py: relax the link regex and resolve relative paths
  back to concept ids via the source doc's directory. Keep a back-compat
  branch for legacy `/`-prefixed links so older in-the-wild bundles
  still produce graph edges.
- prompts/enrichment_instruction.md, prompts/web_ingestion_instruction.md:
  rewrite the Cross-linking section to instruct file-relative links and
  show worked examples from a `tables/<slug>.md` viewpoint.

Tests:
- test_index.py asserts the new emitted form.
- test_viewer.py fixtures use relative links and add a dedicated
  test_legacy_absolute_links_still_resolve case to lock in back-compat.

Bundles (no content edits, link form only):
- okf/bundles/{ga4,stackoverflow,crypto_bitcoin}/**/*.md — 40 files,
  152 link rewrites. Verified bit-for-bit equivalence with a fresh
  `regenerate_indexes` run (sole diff is the synth description, which
  depends on the model).
- toolbox/mdcode/demo/okf/catalog/**/*.md — 7 files, same rewrite. This
  catalog/ is a vendored copy of okf/bundles/ga4/ used by the OKF demo;
  it had drifted from the bundle once the bundle was fixed.

mdcode itself needs no change: documents.ts stores the markdown body
verbatim as the `overview` aspect, so link form does not affect what
gets pushed to Dataplex. The fix is purely about how the .md files
render when browsed as files (GitHub, Obsidian, MkDocs, etc.).

* Drop legacy absolute-link back-compat from viewer

The viewer no longer accepts /-prefixed cross-link targets; only
file-relative paths are resolved. Any older in-the-wild bundle that
still emits /foo.md links will just produce no graph edges for those
links, which is acceptable since the same bundle's links would also
404 on GitHub -- fixing the bundle is the right move, not propping it
up in the viewer.

Removes the back-compat branch in _extract_links and drops the
test_legacy_absolute_links_still_resolve case.

Okf hide manifest (#332)

* okf: move the demo's per-run manifest into a hidden .state/ directory

setup.ts now writes `.state/catalog.yaml`, and push and pull read it from
there. What kcmd sees is unchanged: both still copy the manifest to the root
of the staging tree under its plain name. No command a reader types changes.

`.state/` joins the demo gitignore. The existing `catalog.yaml` line stays,
because the bq and kb demos still write their manifests into their own
directories.

* okf: point the demo README at the manifest's new path

The OKF section told readers to run `cat catalog.yaml`, which no longer
resolves, and described the manifest and cleanup's source by that path.

Okf setup quiet idempotency (#326)

* okf: stop setup.ts printing 409s and discarding real failures

setup.ts created the entry group, the okf aspect type, and the okf-bundle entry type unconditionally, then caught the 409 and updated instead. The result is noise on a successful run and silence on a failed one.

gcloud prints the 409 itself, in red, before the script can react to it. The demo shares the okf aspect type and the okf-bundle entry type across every bundle in a project, and cleanup deliberately leaves both in place, so the second bundle a reader sets up prints two ERROR lines on a run that succeeded.

The catch on the entry group swallowed every other failure along with the 409. A 429 there left the script exiting 0 with catalog.yaml written against an entry group that does not exist. The reader trusts the exit code and moves on with a manifest that points at nothing.

Look each of the three resources up with a describe before deciding what to call. The describe discards its own output and its NOT_FOUND on stderr, so asking the question prints nothing. No create is guarded, so a 429, a permission failure, or any other real error stops the run before the manifest is written.

Verified against a project that already holds the shared types. Two runs with new entry group names print no ERROR line and report both types as updated, and a third run against an existing entry group reuses it. With a 429 injected on the entry group create, the script exits 1 and writes no manifest, where the previous code exited 0 and wrote a manifest naming the missing entry group.

* okf: reword the describe-gate comment in setup.ts as full sentences

okf: harden the demo's defaults, flags, and gcloud calls (#325)

The demo pushed a GA4 sample into a hardcoded okf_ga4 entry group, built
gcloud command lines by string concatenation, and pulled back over the
same directory it pushed from. Each of those is a way to lose work or hit
the wrong project resource.

Default to okf/bundles/acme_retail, the in-repo bundle that exercises the
full v0.2 signal layer. The GA4 sample stays reachable as --bundle catalog.

Parse argv with node:util parseArgs instead of scanning for a flag by
index, so --flag=value works, an unknown or mistyped flag stops the run,
and a missing value is reported rather than silently read as the next
flag. Validate an entry group name against Dataplex's rule before calling
out.

Give --entry-group to setup.ts alone. push, pull, and cleanup read the
entry group back out of the catalog.yaml setup writes, so they cannot be
aimed at an entry group this demo never created, and they stop with a
clear message when that manifest is missing. cleanup names the entry
group and project it is about to delete, since -q skips the prompt.

Pass gcloud an argv array via execFileSync rather than a shell string, so
no value reaches a shell.

Pull writes to ./pulled/, gitignored, instead of over the bundle push
reads from.

the layout could never derive the entry type from it; it stays on the okf
aspect as okf_type and toStaging names the entry type explicitly.

Index files get it too. They carry no frontmatter by SPEC 8, so toStaging
used to pass them through untouched and they fell back to generic, leaving a
bundle's navigation nodes a different kind of thing from the concepts they
link to. They now get a staged type and nothing else. That rules out
requiring the okf aspect on the entry type, since an index has no signal

non-empty regardless: it is what keeps the entry group's own root entry,

okf: carry nested producer-defined keys, and stop leaking .staging (#296)

The `extra` escape hatch only covered top-level frontmatter keys. A
producer-defined subfield inside a modeled record, such as `sources[].license`,
was forwarded to Dataplex verbatim and aborted the push with
ASPECT_SCHEMA_PARSING_FAILURE, so the failure class `extra` was added to close
was still open one level down.

`toStaging` now filters every modeled record against RECORD_KEYS, which until
now was only consulted on the pull side, and diverts whatever it does not name.
Top-level and nested extras share one encoding, a JSON list of [path, value]
pairs, so `fromStaging` restores both by walking the path.

Separately, push.ts and pull.ts removed .staging/ on the line after the kcmd
call, which is skipped when that call throws. A failed push left the tree
behind. Both now clean up in a finally block.

* okf: carry the full v0.2 signal layer through the demo

okf/bundles/acme_retail with "Unknown property: author".

Model the whole v0.2 signal as typed, searchable aspect fields, and carry
producer-defined keys as JSON on an `extra` field, since OKF permits
arbitrary extra keys and no enumerated template can be complete.

Add verify.ts so the translation can be checked without a cloud project,
and --bundle so push/pull/verify can run against a bundle elsewhere in the
repo rather than only the demo's own catalog.

setup.ts now updates an existing aspect type instead of silently skipping

opaque parse error.

locally and through Dataplex, and a GA4 pull after push still leaves the
tree byte-identical.

* okf: drop verify.ts from the demo

Leave correctness checking to the live push/pull round-trip rather than
shipping a second, cloud-free implementation of the same comparison.

okf: stop demo cleanup from deleting the shared okf aspect type (#288)

The okf aspect type is scoped to the project and location, while the
entry group the demo creates is not, so every OKF bundle in the project
carries its signal layer on the same type. Deleting it during cleanup
stripped that signal from bundles the demo does not own, and the bare
catch meant it happened silently. Delete only the entry group and print
the command to remove the aspect type by hand.

issues.title: Partial visibility of sources when a bundle is read across a trust boundary — drop, redact, or reveal?
issues.body:
## Context

§5.1 says a consumer "can judge how much to trust a concept by judging the sources it was extracted from", and §5.3 derives trust tiers from verified alone. Both assume the reader can see the whole of sources.

That holds within one bundle. It does not hold as soon as a bundle, or a store built on OKF documents, is read across a trust boundary (like I do with the Arkeology project) — one team's stable concepts consumed by another team's agents while the working documents they derive from stay internal. E.g. a platform team publishes stable concepts (ADRs, patterns) that other teams' agents read, while its working documents — incident write-ups, drafts, session notes — stay internal. The spec does not describe that setting today, but #15 (imported) already assumes concepts move between bundles, and any shared store of OKF documents meets it immediately. We did.

A published concept, infrastructure, etc. routinely derives from internal material. Its `sources` might then contains entries the authoring team might not want the cross-team reader to have access to — and whose `resource` or `id` may itself be sensitive (`incident-2026-09-01-<customer>-…`). 

But as I understand it, in OKF the `sources` annotation contributes to building a trust framework whose whole idea is "judge a concept by its sources". So deleting internal sources for external customers breaks the trust framework: e.g. a reader see two sources and conclude the document rests on two, when it rests on five. A list that looks complete but isn't is a poor outcome — arguably worse than showing nothing.

The party serving the artifact to the reader has three options, and the spec is silent on which is conformant:

| Option | The reader sees | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Drop** | a shorter list, no trace | the list looks complete and is not — the reader weighs the concept on provenance it does not rest on, which contradicts the §5.1 framing |
| **Reveal** | the full list, links unresolvable | `id`, `resource`, `title` potentially leak information |
| **Redact** | a placeholder entry with no `resource`, `id`, `title` or signals — only that an entry exists and is not visible from here | the reader knows there is provenance they cannot inspect, and nothing more |

## Why this is a spec question rather than a tooling one

A consumer today cannot tell whether a `sources` list it receives is complete: nothing in §5.1 lets an entry say "withheld". So a reader comparing two concepts — one with five visible sources, one with two visible and three withheld — has no way to distinguish *thinly sourced* from *sourced on material I cannot see*, and any §5.3-style trust inference is made on a false premise. The same applies to the `relationships` proposed in #16: a `supersedes` or `builds_on` edge whose target the reader may not see.

## Proposal

Register redaction as the conformant behaviour and give it a shape, so the signal survives the boundary. One possible shape:

```yaml
sources:
  - resource: https://developers.google.com/analytics/bigquery/export-schema
    title: GA4 BigQuery Export schema
  - withheld: 3   # three further entries exist; none is visible from the reader's trust boundary
```

- A single `withheld` entry per list, carrying the count of entries removed and no other key. One placeholder per hidden entry was the alternative; it preserves list positions but leaks the exact number of internal documents one at a time, and the positions carry no meaning once the entries are gone. A count says the one thing the reader needs — how much of the provenance they are not seeing — and nothing else.
- The party serving a partial view MUST emit the marker whenever it removes an entry, and the publisher of the original document decides what is withheld. The spec need not define boundaries or access control — only what a serving party emits when one exists.
- A `withheld` entry MUST NOT be counted as a resolvable source, and a consumer that renders the document or infers trust from it SHOULD show the count next to that judgement — the marker is only useful if the reading end does not drop it.
- Silently dropping an entry is then non-conformant: it misrepresents provenance.

Whether the same key applies to `relationships` can follow #16.

## What we do today

We maintain the [Arkeology](https://github.com/amanoxsolutions/arkeology) tool which can serve several teams from one store of OKF documents and implemented redaction. Own-scope readers see the full list; a reader outside the scope sees the entries they can read plus one marker carrying the count of those they cannot, as proposed above.

One limit is worth stating, because it applies to any implementation of this and shapes what redaction can promise. **The rule governs the frontmatter field, not the body**. An author who writes a withheld source's title into the prose of a shared document has published it, and no gate on `sources` undoes that. We think the line is right rather than a defect. Prose is authored: the writer chose that sentence, in a document they know is shared, and it leaks at most what they typed. The structured field is mechanical: a document synthesised from a dozen internal sources lists a dozen identifiers that no human might read before they were emitted, on every shared document, systematically. Redaction closes the mechanical channel; the authored one remains the author's responsibility, as it is in any sharing system. Redaction's second purpose — telling the reader that the provenance they see is incomplete — does not depend on the body at all, since prose can name a source but cannot say "and there are three more you cannot see". Only the structured field can carry that.

What do you think? Still worth it?

_Note: written with help of AI_

issues.title: Proposal: Evolve OKF into a machine-readable knowledge graph using typed relationships
issues.body:
OKF already forms a graph: concepts are nodes, and Markdown links between concepts create edges. However, the **semantics of those edges are currently expressed in natural-language prose**. A consumer can determine that two concepts are connected, but not what the connection means without interpreting the surrounding Markdown.

**Without machine-readable predicates, OKF represents which resources are connected, but not what those connections mean. It is therefore more precisely a graph of linked resources than a machine-readable semantic knowledge graph.**

This is a problem that **linked data and semantic metadata** have long addressed: not merely linking resources, but making the **meaning of those links machine-readable**. OKF is already close to this model. By adding explicit predicates to its existing links, an OKF bundle could evolve from a collection of interconnected knowledge resources into a lightweight, interoperable knowledge graph.

---

For example, a document may explain that MRR is calculated from subscription data and link to that dataset. Structurally, the consumer sees:

```text
MRR → Subscription Data
```

but the semantic assertion is:

```text
MRR --calculated_from--> Subscription Data
```

## Proposal

Introduce an optional structured representation for typed relations, for example:

```yaml
relations:
  - type: calculated_from
    target: /data/subscriptions.md
```

The containing OKF concept supplies the **subject**, `type` supplies the **predicate**, and `target` supplies the **object**:

```text
(MRR, calculated_from, Subscription Data)
```

This would allow the semantic graph to be reconstructed from structured OKF data without requiring natural-language interpretation.

The intention is **not** to turn OKF into RDF or an ontology language. It is to add the minimal primitive needed to represent explicit semantic assertions between OKF resources.

## Further design

I wrote up the reasoning and further extensions—including directed and symmetric relations, inverse semantics, relation-level provenance, and the boundary between relations, vocabularies, and ontologies—in a separate proposal:

**[[OKF Linked Data proposal](https://github.com/wagner-niklas/okf-linked-data)](https://github.com/wagner-niklas/okf-linked-data)**

I'd appreciate feedback on whether this model fits the intended direction of OKF and how it relates to the existing work around typed relationships.

issues.title: SPEC 6.2 defines a non-slash path-valued field as file-relative, but 6.3, the 10.2/10.3 examples and acme_retail all write them bundle-root-relative (12 of 12)
issues.body:
### Problem

§6.2 defines a path-valued frontmatter field without a leading `/` as **"a relative path"**, i.e. relative to the concept that carries it. But §6.3 and the worked examples in §10 both write **root-relative** paths with no leading slash, and `bundles/acme_retail` follows the examples rather than §6.2.

The two readings disagree for every path-valued field in the reference bundle, so a consumer implementing §6.2 literally finds none of them.

§6.2:

> - an absolute URL (for example `https://...`),
> - a bundle-relative path beginning with `/`, or
> - a relative path (for example `../computations/revenue.md`).

§6.3, describing where executors and attesters point:

> Sources, executors, and attesters commonly point into it (for example `references/attesters/revenue.py`).

§10.2's worked example is a concept at `computations/revenue.md` (per the link in §10.4) carrying:

```yaml
executor:
  resource: references/skills/run-on-bq.md
attester:
  resource: references/attesters/revenue.py
```

and §10.3:

```yaml
computation: references/computations/lib/revenue.sql
```

Read under §6.2, those resolve to `computations/references/skills/run-on-bq.md` and friends — not the bundle-root `references/` directory §6.3 describes.

### Measurement

`bundles/acme_retail`, every path-valued frontmatter field that is neither an absolute URL, nor a §5.1 scope descriptor, nor already `/`-prefixed:

| concept | field | value | file-relative (§6.2) | bundle-root |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `computations/gross-margin-period.md` | `executor.resource` | `skills/run-on-bq.md` | ✗ | ✓ |
| `computations/gross-margin-period.md` | `attester.resource` | `attesters/sql_equality.py` | ✗ | ✓ |
| `computations/gross-margin-period.md` | `sources[].resource` | `policies/margin-standard.md` | ✗ | ✓ |
| `computations/gross-margin-period.md` | `sources[].resource` | `policies/revenue-recognition.md` | ✗ | ✓ |
| `computations/revenue-ytd.md` | `executor.resource` | `skills/run-on-bq.md` | ✗ | ✓ |
| `computations/revenue-ytd.md` | `attester.resource` | `attesters/sql_equality.py` | ✗ | ✓ |
| `computations/revenue-ytd.md` | `sources[].resource` | `policies/revenue-recognition.md` | ✗ | ✓ |
| `computations/revenue-ytd.md` | `sources[].resource` | `tables/orders.md` | ✗ | ✓ |
| `metrics/gross-margin.md` | `sources[].resource` | `policies/margin-standard.md` | ✗ | ✓ |
| `metrics/gross-margin.md` | `sources[].resource` | `policies/revenue-recognition.md` | ✗ | ✓ |
| `metrics/revenue.md` | `sources[].resource` | `policies/revenue-recognition.md` | ✗ | ✓ |
| `tables/orders.md` | `sources[].resource` | `policies/revenue-recognition.md` | ✗ | ✓ |

**12 of 12 resolve at the bundle root. 0 of 12 resolve file-relative.**

The other three bundles (`ga4`, `stackoverflow`, `crypto_bitcoin`) carry no non-`/` path-valued fields at all — every `sources[].resource` there is an absolute URL — so `acme_retail` is the only bundle that exercises this, and it is unanimous.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction — pure path arithmetic, no OKF tooling</summary>

```python
"""Resolve every path-valued frontmatter field two ways:
   file-relative (SPEC 6.2's reading of a non-'/' path) vs bundle-root."""
import os, posixpath, sys, yaml

root = sys.argv[1]
files = {os.path.relpath(os.path.join(dp, fn), root).replace("\\", "/")
         for dp, _, fns in os.walk(root) for fn in fns}

def fm(path):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        t = fh.read()
    if not t.startswith("---"):
        return {}
    return yaml.safe_load(t[3:t.find("\n---", 3)]) or {}

n = fr = rr = 0
for rel in sorted(f for f in files if f.endswith(".md")):
    m = fm(os.path.join(root, rel))
    if not isinstance(m, dict):
        continue
    cand = [(k, m[k]) for k in ("resource", "computation") if isinstance(m.get(k), str)]
    for k in ("executor", "attester"):
        v = m.get(k)
        if isinstance(v, dict) and isinstance(v.get("resource"), str):
            cand.append((k, v["resource"]))
    for s in (m.get("sources") or []):
        if isinstance(s, dict) and isinstance(s.get("resource"), str):
            cand.append(("sources[].resource", s["resource"]))
    for field, raw in cand:
        if "://" in raw or " " in raw or raw.startswith("/"):
            continue   # URL, §5.1 scope descriptor, or unambiguous
        n += 1
        fr += posixpath.normpath(posixpath.join(posixpath.dirname(rel), raw)) in files
        rr += posixpath.normpath(raw) in files
print(f"non-'/' fields: {n}  file-relative: {fr}  bundle-root: {rr}")
```

```
$ python okf_paths.py bundles/acme_retail
non-'/' fields: 12  file-relative: 0  bundle-root: 12
```

Checked against `ad30107`.
</details>

### Why it matters

These fields carry the derivation and execution edges, and they appear nowhere in the body prose — so they are invisible to any consumer that only parses Markdown links. A consumer that resolves them per §6.2 gets nothing: in `acme_retail`, every `Attested Computation → policy it implements` edge, every `→ table it reads`, and every `→ executor / attester` is dropped.

Concretely, "what depends on the revenue recognition policy" is answerable only from `policies/index.md`, even though four concepts declare a dependency on it in frontmatter.

### Possible resolutions

Either direction resolves it; the ambiguity is the problem, not the choice:

1. **Clarify §6.2** so path-valued fields resolve against the bundle root regardless of a leading slash — matching §6.3 and the §10 examples and requiring no change to the bundles. If so, it is worth saying explicitly that §6.2 differs from §6.1 here, since body links and frontmatter paths would then resolve differently.
2. **Keep §6.2 as written** and prefix the paths in `bundles/acme_retail`, the §10.2/§10.3 examples, and §6.3's example with `/`.

A permissive consumer can try §6.2 and fall back to the root, which is what I ended up doing, but that is a guess: it means the same string in two bundles can denote two different files, and there is no way to tell which the producer meant.

### Not a duplicate of #14

#14 concerns §6.1 **body Markdown links** in the reference viewer. This is about §6.2 **frontmatter path-valued fields**, where the spec's own definition and its own examples disagree. The two are independent — `acme_retail` body links *are* `/`-prefixed, which is what makes the frontmatter convention stand out.

issues.title: Proposal: Keep `generated` for what it means and add `revised` or `edited` key
issues.body:
## Problem

**`generated` does not record when the concept was generated.** §5.2 defines:
> _`generated.at:` An ISO 8601 datetime marking the content's last meaningful change. Consumers use it to tell a recent edit from a stale fact._

The name and the semantic of the `generated` key point in opposite directions: generation vs last edition.

Also the `generated.by` half is overloaded too, and that one loses information. A concept first
written by an agent and later edited by a human must, on that edit, move `generated.by` to the human — because `generated` is the last-change record. The *producer* of the content is then unrecoverable from the bundle. A consumer can no longer distinguish:

- a concept a human wrote, from
- a concept an agent generated that a human later touched.

That is a trust-relevant distinction, and it is precisely the kind of distinction §5.3's tiers exist to preserve. `verified` answers "who confirmed it"; nothing
answers "who produced it" once anyone edits.

## Why `verified` does not help to track revisions

`verified` is a useful key but the wrong event to record edits/revisions: §5.2 says it records *confirmation*, explicitly independent of `generated.at`. An edit is neither a generation nor a confirmation. There is no place to put it.

## Proposal (edited)

_Note: the original proposal has been updated based on the discussion inside this thread._

Let `generated` and `verified` mean what they says, and give edits/revisions their own key:

```yaml
generated: { by: reference_agent/gemini-2.5-pro, at: 2026-06-20T22:53:05Z }
revised: { by: human:bob, at: 2026-07-02T11:00:00Z } 
verified:
  - { by: human:ahormati, at: 2026-06-25T09:00:00Z }
  - { by: process:finance-nightly, at: 2026-06-26T02:00:00Z }
```

- generated — unchanged shape, by REQUIRED; now means when and by whom the content was produced, and is never rewritten.
- verified — unchanged shape and meaning
- revised — OPTIONAL `{ by, at }` last revision event, mirroring generated exactly: same actor convention (§7), same ISO 8601 rule. The value is overwritten in place at each revision. `revised` older than `last_verified` is an advisory signal, as following §5.2 content can change without re-verification.

Meaning the above artifact

- was first authored on 2026-06-20 by reference_agent/gemini-2.5-pro
- later verified twice on 2026-06-25 and 2026-06-26 by 2 different parties
- then modified on 2026-07-02T11 by human:bob
- and is unverified since it was updated

Freshness becomes the latest between generated and revised — the same "how recently" rule §5.2 already states for verified, applied to one more family.

## Backwards compatibility

Close to free, and conservative in the safe direction:

- revised is OPTIONAL. Absent, generated.at is the only timestamp, which is what every v0.2 bundle written so far already means. Existing bundles stay valid.
- A consumer that ignores revised computes an older freshness than the truth. It can never report a concept as fresher than it is — the same conservative property #15 argues for with imported.
- No new actor forms, no new heading, no change to §5.3's tier derivation.
- The one genuine change is to `generated.at`'s definition for producers who already write last-change into it. Because freshness is computed as the latest at and those bundles carry no revised, the computed answer is unchanged — only the "when was this produced" reading differs, and that is a question no current bundle can answer anyway.

## Background

We have adopted OKF 0.1 for our own Agentic Software Development framework and its corpus of planning documents — brainstorming sessions, specs, decision records, code reviews,... — authored by agents and revised across sessions, where "who first produced this and when" and "who last touched it" are routinely different actors and both are worth keeping.
We are also authoring an open source MCP tool [Arkeology](https://github.com/amanoxsolutions/arkeology), to store all artifacts outside Git and provide agents semantic search rather that an index.md file with description which can't capture a full artifact rich content and use all OKF metadata for search filtering.
We kept a house authored/revised pair through v0.1 and expected v0.2 to absorb it. generated looked like the home for authored by name, and turned out to be the home for revised by definition, so we are carrying all three rather than lose the producer. Happy to be told we have misread the intent.

issues.title: Support YAML metadata in a leading HTML comment for GitHub Wiki compatibility
issues.body:
Following the [request to separate this proposal from #9](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/open-knowledge-format/issues/9#issuecomment-5650324697), could OKF support a clearly identified leading HTML comment as an optional alternative to YAML frontmatter? ## Why this matters GitHub Wiki maintainers could keep one set of Markdown files for human-readable documentation and OKF consumers, without adding visible metadata to page headings or navigation or maintaining a separate export. Conventional frontmatter would remain available wherever visible metadata is desirable. ## GitHub Wiki rendering Conventional `---` frontmatter renders as a horizontal rule and a large H2 containing the YAML in both the published page and custom sidebar (`_Sidebar.md`). Wrapping the same metadata in `` hides it from the rendered page and sidebar. The original headings, anchors, and nested navigation remain intact; the metadata remains in the saved Markdown.
Screenshot: conventional YAML adds visible metadata [View the published YAML example](https://github.com/Ayanmullick/test/wiki/OKF-YAML-Frontmatter).
Screenshot: HTML comments preserve clean rendering [View the published HTML-comment example](https://github.com/Ayanmullick/test/wiki/OKF-HTML-Comment).
Reproduction steps and Markdown examples Save the following as a GitHub Wiki Markdown page and view the published page: ```markdown --- type: Guide title: Project Wiki description: Guides and API documentation. tags: [documentation, api] --- # Project Wiki - [API Guide](#api-guide) - [API Reference](#api-reference) ## API Guide Read the guide and explore the reference below. ### API Reference Use the documented commands and examples. ``` Replace only its leading metadata block with: ```markdown ``` The same comparison applies to `_Sidebar.md`: prepend each metadata form to a list with an indented child link. The screenshots show both the page and narrow custom sidebar. Example pages: [conventional YAML](https://github.com/Ayanmullick/test/wiki/OKF-YAML-Frontmatter) and [HTML comment](https://github.com/Ayanmullick/test/wiki/OKF-HTML-Comment).
GitHub documentation and rendering references - [Wiki rendering](https://docs.github.com/en/communities/documenting-your-project-with-wikis/adding-or-editing-wiki-pages#about-wiki-filenames): Markdown Wiki files use GitHub's Markdown converter. - [Hiding content with HTML comments](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/getting-started-with-writing-and-formatting-on-github/basic-writing-and-formatting-syntax#hiding-content-with-comments): commented content is omitted from rendered Markdown. - [YAML metadata in documents](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/viewing-yaml-metadata-in-your-documents/): describes metadata tables for prose documents generally. The Wiki behavior above differs from that presentation.
## Suggested scope - Keep conventional frontmatter; allow an explicit, document-start comment marker as an alternative, rather than interpreting arbitrary comments. - Retain the same metadata fields and validation, including non-empty `type`. - Define handling for duplicate/conflicting blocks, malformed comments, and YAML values containing HTML-comment delimiters. - Require consumers to read raw Markdown; hiding metadata is presentation control, not confidentiality. Would you consider extending the [OKF specification](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/open-knowledge-format/blob/main/SPEC.md) to support this optional HTML-comment syntax, so GitHub Wikis can be OKF-compliant without displaying metadata to readers?

issues.title: Proposal: producing a bundle in parts — reserved filenames collide on merge, and a regenerated bundle-root `index.md` may drop `okf_version`
issues.body:
## Summary

For disclosure: we are not blocked. We produce a bundle of roughly 10,000 concepts in about 100 parts, one zip per part, under v0.2 as written. This issue records where the spec is silent about that workflow and proposes two independent things, either acceptable alone: **one sentence in §8** and **one informative subsection §3.2** in the style of §10.5. No new key, reserved filename, or §11 item. It touches the same file as #11 and the same key as #24 (see *Related*); a fix for the reference-implementation side of gap 1 is proposed in PR #25.

## What already works

- Parts can omit `index.md`: §3 marks it Optional, §8 says it MAY appear, §11 constrains it only "when present" and forbids rejecting a bundle for "Missing `index.md` files". §8 already says "Producers MAY generate `index.md` automatically", and the reference agent regenerates them at the end of every `enrich` (`src/reference_agent/runner.py:297-298`).
- A link into a part not yet merged is broken until then; §6.1 says such a link "is not malformed" and consumers MUST tolerate it.

## Gaps

1. **A regenerated bundle-root `index.md` may lose `okf_version`.** §8 permits `okf_version` only in the bundle-root `index.md` (§12 cross-references this) and lets producers generate `index.md`; nothing says what a producer that rewrites an existing bundle-root `index.md` does with the key. The reference implementation drops it: `regenerate_indexes()` never reads the existing file (`src/reference_agent/bundle/index.py:85-86`) and writes headings and bullets only (`index.py:35-48`, `:103-104`). Reproduced on a copy of `bundles/acme_retail` at `ad30107` with `okf_version: "0.2"` added: gone after one run. Nothing in the repository writes or reads the key today, so the loss is invisible until a bundle declares one.
2. **Reserved filenames collide on merge.** Two parts that both carry an `index.md` or `log.md` at the same path cannot both survive extraction into one root; the last one written wins silently. Nothing forbids regenerating `index.md` (§8), but §8 ties `okf_version` to that file and does not say whether listing content that no frontmatter supplies (the subdirectory descriptions in `bundles/acme_retail/index.md`, a form §8's own template sanctions) is authoritative. §9 fixes the shape of `log.md` but not how two logs for one scope combine.
3. **Same path, different content.** A concept's ID is "the path of the concept's file within the bundle, with the `.md` suffix removed" (§2); nothing says what a merge does when two parts carry the same concept path. That state exists only inside the merge step, never in a bundle, which is why the text below is informative.

## Proposal 1: one sentence in §8

After "Producers MAY generate `index.md` automatically; consumers MAY synthesize one on the fly when none is present." (the end of §8) add, in the idiom of §4.1's "Consumers SHOULD preserve unknown keys when round-tripping":

> A producer that regenerates a bundle-root `index.md` SHOULD preserve an existing `okf_version` key unless it declares a different version.

It qualifies the generation permission it follows and does not declare `index.md` derived: `bundles/acme_retail/index.md` carries hand-written subdirectory descriptions that exist in no frontmatter, and `regenerate_indexes()` replaces them (open question 1).

## Proposal 2: informative §3.2

**Update, 2026-09-14.** Proposal 2's third bullet revised and split in two after the review below; the clause it replaced read: "the merging producer may write those `index.md` and `log.md` files afterwards (§8, §9)".

> ### 3.2 Producing a bundle in parts (informative)
>
> This subsection is informative, not normative.
>
> A producer may write a bundle as several *parts* that are merged later, for example one part per batch of an export pipeline. A part is a directory tree rooted at the bundle root, holding a subset of the bundle's files at their bundle paths; it is a fragment of one bundle rather than a bundle of its own (§2), and a concept's path and concept ID (§2) are the same in the part and in the merged bundle. The conditions in §11 apply file by file, so a part can be checked before it is merged; links into parts not yet merged are broken until then (§6.1).
>
> Merging is a union: a part asserts the concepts it contains and says nothing about those it omits, so it cannot express that a concept was removed or renamed. Recording a removal is not addressed here.
>
> - Derive each concept's path from a stable identifier of what it describes, unique across parts, so that re-running a part writes the same paths. Do not rely on letter case to keep paths distinct: a case-folding filesystem drops one file silently; comparing case-folded paths across parts before extraction catches this.
> - The merging producer takes one version of each part (which parts exist and which paths each writes is producer bookkeeping that OKF does not specify); a later run replaces that part's earlier output at those paths, including any `verified` events (§5.2) or `status` (§5.4) added to the merged bundle after the earlier merge. The same concept path in two parts with different content is a conflict: keeping one copy silently loses knowledge, so fail or report it. Identical copies are not a conflict.
> - A part contributes to every directory at or above the files it writes, including the bundle root. Keep reserved filenames (§3.1) out of directories that more than one part contributes to; any `index.md` or `log.md` there is written by the merging producer, after merging (§8, §9). All parts of one bundle target the same OKF version; a merged bundle's `okf_version`, if declared, is written by the merging producer (§12).
> - Such a file can hold more than the parts supply. What the parts do supply, such as an `index.md` listing built from frontmatter, a later merge can regenerate (§8). What no part can restate, the merging producer carries forward, from the existing file or from its own bookkeeping: the `okf_version` key of a bundle-root `index.md` (§12), and any `log.md` entry the current merge did not itself write, whether an earlier merge or a later editor put it there, since a `log.md` records the history of changes to its scope (§9) and an entry there can state a decision about the bundle as a whole. A file rebuilt from the parts alone drops such content silently, since §11 checks only a reserved file's structure.
>
> How a part ships is a producer choice; §3 specifies distribution forms only for a whole bundle, and OKF does not specify manifests or checksums (§1 leaves such conventions to the producer).

## Backwards compatibility

Additive. No new reserved filename, frontmatter key, or §11 item. §3.2 contains no MUST, SHOULD or MAY, like §10.5. The one keyword, the SHOULD in §8, binds only a producer that regenerates a bundle-root `index.md`; every bundle and consumer conformant today stays conformant. Whether this goes into 0.2 in place or waits for a 0.3 line is your call; §12 counts additions as a minor bump, and #24 raises the same question for PR #6.

## Alternatives considered

- **Each batch as its own subtree** (`batches/0017/...`): concept IDs would encode batch numbers, which carry no meaning for the knowledge itself.
- **Standardizing a part manifest.** OKF defines no manifest. One producer ships a machine index inside the bundle root (comment on #11, `bundle/.manifest.json`); a part manifest describes one archive and is read by the merging producer, not by a consumer of the merged bundle. We propose nothing.

## Related

- #24 asks what the value `okf_version: "0.2"` identifies after PR #6; this issue asks whether the key survives regeneration of `index.md`. Orthogonal to each of #24's resolutions.
- #11 proposes that `index.md` (or another discovery surface) carry entries for removed concepts, which are not derivable from present concepts. Hence §3.2's union with removal left to #11, and a §8 sentence that preserves a key rather than declaring `index.md` derived.
- #14: a non-reference producer reports that a predecessor format lost 104 notes silently to filename collisions on a case-folding filesystem, the reason for the letter-case sentence.
- PR #25: proposed reference fix for gap 1.

## Open questions

1. How should a producer that regenerates `index.md` treat a hand-authored one such as `bundles/acme_retail/index.md`, whose subdirectory descriptions exist nowhere else? §8 permits only `okf_version` in `index.md` frontmatter, so a marker key would change §8, which §11 item 3 makes a conformance condition, and is not proposed; #10's topic-lead concept could give directory descriptions a frontmatter home, and a leading generator comment (`<!-- generated by <actor> -->`) may fit §8 as written.
2. Should `okf_version` be declarable outside the bundle-root `index.md`, so it is not tied to a file producers MAY generate? (Orthogonal to #24, which concerns the value, not the location.)

Happy to send a PR with the wording if this is the direction you prefer.

issues.title: index: preserve root index.md okf_version on regeneration
issues.body:
`regenerate_indexes()` rewrites every `index.md` from scratch and never reads the existing file, so an `okf_version` declared in the bundle-root `index.md` — the only place SPEC.md §8/§12 allow it — is dropped on every `enrich` run (`runner.py` calls it at the end of `enrich_all`).

This change reads the existing bundle-root `index.md` before rewriting it and re-emits its `okf_version` key ahead of the regenerated listing. Only that key is carried, and only at the bundle root; every other `index.md` stays frontmatter-free, as §8 requires.

Reproduced on a copy of `bundles/acme_retail` at ad30107 with `okf_version: "0.2"` added to the root `index.md`: before this change the key is gone after one run; after it, it survives.

Notes:

- `yaml.safe_dump` renders the value as `okf_version: '0.2'` (single quotes); that is the same YAML string as the spec's `"0.2"`.
- The listing itself is still regenerated from frontmatter, so hand-written index text is still replaced. That behaviour is unchanged here.
- Test: `tests/test_index.py::test_regenerate_preserves_root_okf_version`. Full suite: 40 passed.

Related to #26 (gap 1 there is the behaviour this fixes).

issues.title: `okf_version: "0.2"` now names two documents: #6's explicit-offset requirement is breaking but carries no version bump
issues.body:
PR #6 (merged 2026-08-21, `ad30107c`) inserted at `SPEC.md:284`:

> Every timestamp-valued key in OKF is an ISO 8601 datetime with an explicit UTC offset, for example `2026-06-30T14:00:00Z`.

and rewrote three keys that §5 had previously specified as `YYYY-MM-DD`: `stale_after`, `sources[].last_modified`, and `usage_window.{from,to}`. The prose carrying the old form went with it — `stale_after` lost "An absolute date (`YYYY-MM-DD`)" and `last_modified` lost its parenthetical. So `stale_after: 2026-09-23` was normative before that commit and is non-conformant after it.

§12 (`SPEC.md:768-775`) reserves breaking changes for a major bump, minor bumps being backward-compatible additions. `SPEC.md:3` reads **Version 0.2** both before the change and after it.

**Consequence.** Two bundles both declaring `okf_version: "0.2"` can now legitimately disagree about whether `stale_after: 2026-09-23` is conformant, so a conformance claim against "0.2" is not a well-defined statement — a consumer reading that declaration cannot tell which of the two documents the producer built against.

I am not assuming this was an oversight. A pre-1.0 correction to a format still settling is reasonable on its own terms; it is the version string that is now carrying two meanings.

Several ways to resolve it, any of which would do, and the choice is yours:

- A version bump, so the document states which revision it is.
- An errata note in §13, which already sets the precedent of naming v0.1's breaking changes explicitly.
- A commit- or date-qualified spec identifier, so `okf_version` resolves to bytes rather than to a moving reference.
- If compatibility was the intent: a sentence saying consumers SHOULD accept a date-only value for these three keys and read it as midnight UTC. That is one clause, and it makes every bundle written before 21 August conformant again.

**Where we sit**, for disclosure: not blocked, and not raising this because it cost us anything. We pin `ad30107c` in our interoperability fixtures rather than resolving a version string, and we emit none of the three affected keys, so we cannot produce the old form even by accident. I am raising it for implementations that pin by version string instead of by commit, where the two readings differ with nothing to signal it.

Happy to send a PR for the last option if that is the direction you would prefer.

issues.title: Proposal: register query-time semantics for `supersedes` and `contested_by` on the #16 carrier
issues.body:
#16 gives relationships a carrier: `to`, `type`, `direction`, and the §5.3 trust shapes one level down. It deliberately leaves `type` producer-defined and unconstrained, and that is the right call for the carrier. This proposes the other half for two specific types, because a consumer reading `type: supersedes` still cannot tell whether to drop the target from an in-force query.

Two lifecycle edges, each with its query-time semantics registered beside it. They differ on the axis that drives consumer behaviour: **directionality**.

*Revised 2026-09-14 from review by @ajdelaguila and @3a3; the comment thread carries the derivation.*

## The two types

| | `supersedes` | `contradicts` |
|---|---|---|
| Symmetry | **Asymmetric.** The carrying concept replaces the referenced one. | **Semantically symmetric, stored one-sided.** Written on the asserting concept only; the reverse is derived. |
| Direction | Backward in time, to the concept being replaced. | Outbound from the asserting concept. `direction` reads as it does for any asymmetric type. |
| Query-time | **Exclude, once affirmed.** Drop the superseded concept from in-force retrieval; retain it in the bundle for lineage. | **Surface both.** Never resolve the edge as a verdict, collapse "contested" into "false", or drop a side without human or higher-signal input. |
| Encodes a verdict? | Once affirmed, yes. | **No.** Records that a dispute exists, never who is right. |
| Inverse emitted? | **No.** Resolution keys on the forward edge only. An inverse spelling gives a producer two ways to state one relationship and a consumer two places to look, which is how a reversed edge survives review (@jpavley shipped one inverted, `GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog#148`). | **Derived, never written.** See the naming section. |
| Dangling target | Not an error. If the target is absent, the carrying concept is current. | Not an error. |

```yaml
relationships:
  - to: remember://lesson/lesson-corpus-est-000
    type: supersedes
    generated: { by: remember/0.2, at: 2026-09-12T09:00:00Z }
```

Targets are stable concept ids per `GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog#120`, not paths, so a file move cannot reattach an edge to the wrong incumbent. @pixie79 reports the same conclusion from the other end on #16: deriving a concept's path from its key guessed wrong for 43 links on a real render, each a valid-looking path to a file that did not exist.

## Naming: one stored key, one derived view

- **`contradicts`** is the stored key, on the asserting concept, one side only.
- **`contradicted_by`** is the derived reverse view, computed at read time and **never written to frontmatter**.
- **`contested_by`** is a deprecated spelling. Consumers SHOULD read it as `contradicts`.

Under one-sided storage `contested_by` is inverted: the asserter would carry a key saying it *is* contested, the reverse of what it asserts. This registration, @inkxel's implementation and Data Olympus's are then one vocabulary rather than three. We ship `contested_by` today and have the migration to do.

A mirror write, with both records carrying the edge, is a two-write that can half-apply, and a one-sided contest is a different condition from the dangling target ruled benign above. Derivation costs a consumer nothing that it is not already paying: a reverse index over stable ids is what resolves targets at all.

## Three rungs, and only the third authorizes exclusion

With `verified` and `generated` available on the edge it is tempting to read edge provenance as authorization. It is not, and neither is the middle rung.

1. **Edge provenance** - `generated` / `verified` on the relationship. Says who asserted the edge. Authorizes nothing. @pixie79 confirms the carrier claims no more: "our edges carry `kind`, `provenance` and `confidence`, and none of that is an affirmation."
2. **Source eligibility** - the asserting concept is itself in force. Data Olympus ships this: an in-force query excludes the target of a `supersedes` edge whose source is in force, an edge asserted from an inbox document excludes nothing whatever status it claims, and a dangling edge excludes nothing because the join needs both ends to resolve.
3. **Attributed resolution** - someone affirmed *this* retirement, recorded as an appended, attributed event.

**Exclusion follows affirmation.** An automated writer may propose a supersession; the incumbent keeps governing until the resolution event is recorded. Rung 2 is weaker than rung 3 and is named rather than collapsed into it, because it is what a real implementation runs today: source eligibility says the edge comes from something currently governing, it does not say anyone affirmed this particular retirement. That distinction is what a consumer needs when 18,803 of 19,349 edges are derived.

**Exclusion requires both.** A present forward edge **and** a readable affirmation, together. An affirmation surviving in `log.md` after the edge is removed from the successor, or after the successor leaves the bundle, is incomplete evidence, so the incumbent stays in force.

## The resolution event

**Where it lives: the bundle-root `log.md`.** Nearest-ancestor would make the in-force answer depend on where a concept sits in the tree, so a file move could change which log governs its retirement, contradicting the stable-id rule above. **A resolution entry in a non-root `log.md` is not an affirmation**; §9 permits the file at any level, and an entry elsewhere excludes nothing.

**§9 supplies the file's shape and no preservation duty** (`SPEC.md:535-552`), so the append-only behaviour this registration depends on is the producer's to supply, not the format's. For a bundle assembled in parts that producer is the merging one: it writes root reserved files after merging and carries forward every `log.md` entry it did not write, from the existing file or from its own bookkeeping. @3a3's #26 §3.2 now states this (revised 2026-09-14); their merge becomes read-then-add, keeping each such entry unchanged under its original date heading.

**Entry shape**, in §9's own idiom - its `**Update**` / `**Creation**` / `**Deprecation**` convention, made normative inside this registration rather than in core:

```markdown
## 2026-09-14
* **Supersession**: `remember://lesson/b` supersedes `remember://lesson/a`. Affirmed by `human:1c8998e4`.
* **Dismissal**: contest between `remember://lesson/c` and `remember://lesson/d` dismissed. Affirmed by `human:1c8998e4`.
```

A consumer MUST find four things: the disposition word, both stable concept ids, and the attributing actor in §7's form. The date comes from the enclosing §9 heading.

**Absent, malformed or undecidable evidence fails safe.** If any of the four is missing or unparseable, the entry is not a readable affirmation, so the incumbent stays in force and nothing is excluded. The same answer covers conflicting entries: §9 orders dates newest first and says nothing about order inside a date, so two conflicting entries on one pair under one heading are not decisive. This also answers a real adoption case - @pixie79 reports on #16 that Roteiro populates no author fields and discards a peer's `author` on import. That producer excludes nothing rather than excluding wrongly, and needs no change to stay conformant.

**Where the conformance layer lands: in this registration, not §11.** Core should not carry a clause for a community extension it does not define. A consumer implementing this registration gets a checkable bar; a bundle that ignores the registration is unaffected.

## Three states, read from the bundle alone

No adjudication engine, no edited records, every resolution an append.

1. **Never questioned** - no `contradicts` pointing at it, not the target of any `supersedes`. Absence means no dispute asserted, not proven undisputed.
2. **Contested and open** - the edge exists, both concepts present, no resolution recorded. Surface both.
3. **Contested and settled** - a resolution is recorded, not edited in. The `contradicts` edge is **retained whatever the disposition**, so a settled contest stays distinguishable from one never raised. Drop it and a reader returning later cannot tell a question that was settled from one that was never asked.

A `supersedes` edge with no resolution event yet is a proposal, not a fourth state: both concepts surface and the incumbent stays in force.

Settlement comes two ways.

**Supersession** - the winner gains the `supersedes` edge, the loser's validity window closes, both retain `contradicts`, and exclusion keys on the resolution entry rather than on the closed window. A closed window with no entry is decay, and reading it as affirmation would collapse decay and affirmed supersession into one, which is the silent displacement the invariant forbids.

**Dismissal withdraws the contest, not a concept.** No window closes, both concepts stay in force, and the entry's whole job is moving the pair from contested-and-open to contested-and-settled. A concept examined and judged wrong is #13's `refuted` or a supersession; dismissal is not a third way to retire something, and `contradicts` carries no verdict by design.

## Composition

- **§5.4 `status`** says whether a concept is current; the edge says where current lives. Neither implies the other, and a consumer that understands only one still behaves correctly. §5.4 defines `deprecated` as kept for links and history, but nothing in frontmatter points from a deprecated concept to its replacement, so a consumer filtering out deprecated concepts drops the only breadcrumb at the moment it acts on the signal.
- **§5.3 trust tiers** derive from `verified`, and §10.6 makes verification doc-level and recorded in the bundle, so a concept human-reviewed in June can be contested in July with its tier intact. A tier-filtering consumer surfaces it as human-reviewed and never sees the dispute unless the contest is typed.
- **#13 (`refuted`)** is a trust event on a concept that exists; these are relations between concepts. `contradicts` defers adjudication by design and carries no verdict, so it does not overlap.
- **#15 (`imported`)** composes: an imported relationship reports the upstream's tier without inheriting it.
- **#11 (deletion semantics)** is the presence axis. A superseded concept stays in the bundle; a removed one needs an absence record.
- **#26 (bundles in parts)** carries the merge-side obligation this registration depends on.

**Floor for partial implementation.** A consumer that implements the carrier and not this registration excludes nothing. Under exclusion follows affirmation that is the designed failure direction, not an accident.

## Provenance

Two production implementations, arrived at independently. Ours ships both keys in the *remember* exporter with the sample bundle at https://github.com/andrewcrenshaw/remember-okf-sample-bundle. @ajdelaguila's Data Olympus ships source-gated supersession over concept ids and holds `contradicts` as annotation that never filters, with contest disposition open at knaisoma/data-olympus#241. The two differ on one mechanism: Data Olympus reads a contest-to-supersession count out of git diffs, and we record a resolution event at settlement so the same count is a query. That difference is the argument for rung 3.

The prior text, with the extended composition and a worked sample bundle, was `GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog#195`, now retired in favour of this. Its own adjacent-proposals section predicted this carrier: a broader carrier for producer-defined relations can host these two edges without redefining them, because the query-time semantics attach to the relation and not to the syntax.

Glad to take further convergence edits here and then put it up as a PR.

issues.title: viewer: render footnote attribution via marked-footnote
issues.body:
## Problem

The bundle viewer renders card bodies with `marked.parse(body, { gfm: true })` (`static/viz.js`). marked's GFM support does not include footnotes — but the spec's per-claim attribution mechanism is markdown footnotes keyed to `sources` entries. So a card that follows the spec's own attribution convention shows its `[^id]` markers as literal text in the viewer's detail panel.

## Fix (two lines)

- `src/reference_agent/viewer/templates/viz.html`: load the UMD build of [marked-footnote](https://github.com/bent10/marked-extensions/tree/main/packages/footnote) from jsdelivr, next to the existing cytoscape/marked CDN scripts;
- `src/reference_agent/viewer/static/viz.js`: `if (window.markedFootnote) { marked.use(markedFootnote()); }` as the first statement of the viewer IIFE.

`[^id]` markers now render as a superscript reference plus the definition block at the end of the body. The guard keeps the viewer working unchanged when the script cannot load (e.g. offline). Pre-generated `bundles/*/viz.html` pick this up the next time they are regenerated.

## Verification

Generated a viewer for a small bundle whose concept body uses `[^spec]` footnote attribution and opened the result: the reference renders as a link, the definition renders as a footnote block, and the graph/sources/backlinks panels are unaffected. With no network access to the CDN the page behaves exactly as before.
